FLEET REPAIR-OR-REPLACE PLANNER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Is it cheaper to repair or replace it this year?

Add one row per van, truck or machine you are deciding about. The planner costs out keeping it — last year's repair spend plus the revenue you lost on the days it was off the road — against replacing it, then ranks the whole fleet by annual saving per dollar of capital and fills the budget you have.

The repair invoices are the visible number and usually the smaller one. See why downtime decides this for the two-minute version.

Nothing is uploaded. Your figures are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer. Weighing a lease buyout instead of a cash purchase? The equipment lease buyout calculator does that one asset in more depth; this page decides which of several assets to act on at all.

This planner vs. paid fleet management software — what a per-vehicle monthly subscription tracks that this free worksheet does not, and does.

This planner vs. a spreadsheet — the two formulas a hand-built version most often gets wrong, and what runs the same way every time here.

This planner vs. comparing the repair bill to a new price — what the default comparison leaves out.

Add a vehicle or machine

This year's capital budget

What you can actually spend on replacements this year. Leave it at 0 for no stated limit — every asset that pays will then be selected.

The plan

No assets added yet — add one above, or load the example.

AssetKeep / yearReplace / yearAnnual savingCapitalPaybackVerdictIn plan

What this does and doesn't do

Keeping an asset costs you its repair spend plus the revenue lost on the days it was out of service. Replacing it costs you the net capital that actually leaves the business — replacement price minus trade-in — spread straight-line over the years of service you expect, plus what the replacement still costs to run. Replacing wins when the first total is larger.

It does not appraise your equipment, know your tax position, depreciation schedule or financing terms, or model interest, inflation and the time value of money. The budget ranking is a heuristic — annual saving per dollar of capital, filled in that order — not a guaranteed-optimal subset. Confirm every quote and trade-in figure in writing before committing capital.

The assumptions, stated

    Common questions

    Is it cheaper to repair or replace a work truck?

    It depends on two numbers most owners compare and one they usually leave out. Repairing costs you the annual repair spend plus the revenue lost on the days the vehicle is off the road. Replacing costs you the net capital you lay out (replacement price minus trade-in) spread over the years of service it buys, plus whatever the new vehicle still costs to run. Replacing is cheaper when the first total is larger than the second. The number that gets left out is downtime: a van in the shop is billable days your crew could not work, and for a crew billing several hundred dollars a day that frequently exceeds the repair invoice that got all the attention.

    How do you work out the annual cost of replacing a vehicle?

    Take the replacement price, subtract the trade-in or resale value to get the net capital actually leaving the business, and divide that by the number of years of service you expect from the replacement. That gives an equivalent annual cost for the capital. Then add the running costs the new asset still has — its own expected repairs and any downtime you still expect. This planner does that arithmetic straight-line and undiscounted, so you can check it on paper; it does not model financing interest, so add your own cost of borrowing if you would finance the purchase.

    What is a good payback period on replacing equipment?

    Payback is the net capital divided by the annual repair and downtime spend that replacing stops — the cash you actually stop paying out, not the equivalent-annual-cost comparison, which already has the capital inside it. This planner calls out anything paying back inside three years as a strong case, because that is comfortably inside the service life of most vehicles and machines and leaves room for the input estimates to be somewhat wrong. A payback longer than the expected service life means the asset does not pay to replace on these numbers at all. Payback deliberately ignores the time value of money, so treat it as a screening measure rather than a financing decision.

    How do I choose which vehicles to replace when I cannot afford all of them?

    Rank them by annual saving per dollar of capital rather than by the size of the saving or the age of the asset. An older vehicle with a large repair bill can still be the wrong one to replace first if the replacement is expensive and the trade-in is worthless. This planner sorts your assets that way and fills the capital budget you enter in that order, then shows what deferring the rest costs you per year so you can weigh it against what the extra capital would cost to borrow.

    Is this planner financial advice?

    No. It performs arithmetic on the numbers you enter. It does not appraise your equipment, does not know your tax position, depreciation schedule or financing terms, and does not decide anything on your behalf. Confirm replacement quotes and trade-in values in writing and take the worksheet, not the recommendation, to whoever advises you.

    No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. is-it-cheaper-to-repair-or-replace-a-wor.text:
← Back to the repair-or-replace planner

Is it cheaper to repair or replace a work truck?

Almost everybody compares two numbers: what the repairs cost last year, and what a new one costs. That comparison leaves out the number that usually decides it.

The missing number is the days it was off the road

A van in the shop is not just an invoice. It is billable days your crew could not work — or a rental, or a job that went to somebody else, or a customer who did not call back. None of that appears on the repair bill, which is exactly why it gets left out: the invoice arrives in the post and the lost day does not.

Put a number on it. If a two-person crew bills $900 on a normal day and the van was out for eleven days, keeping that van cost you 11 × $900 = $9,900 in lost revenue on top of whatever the garage charged. For a lot of ageing vehicles that figure is several times the repair spend that got all the attention.

So the real cost of keeping an asset for another year is:

keep = annual repair spend + (downtime days × what a day costs you)

Use the revenue a day actually costs you, not your day rate on paper. If you can shuffle work to another van and lose nothing, the number is low. If the van going down stops a crew, it is the crew's whole day.

The cost of replacing is not the sticker price

Buying a $42,000 van does not cost you $42,000 this year. Two things change that.

First, the trade-in comes off. What actually leaves the business is the net capital: replacement price minus whatever the old one is worth. Second, that capital buys you several years of service, so charging all of it against one year overstates it badly. Spread it over the years of service you expect:

replace = (replacement price - trade-in) / expected years
          + the replacement's own annual repairs
          + (its expected downtime days × what a day costs you)

That middle line is an equivalent annual cost. The last two lines matter because a replacement is not free to run — a new van still needs servicing and will still be off the road occasionally, and pretending otherwise flatters the replacement case.

Replacing is cheaper when keep is bigger than replace. The difference is your annual saving.

A worked example

A 2014 Transit: $6,400 of repairs last year and fourteen days off the road, with a day costing $900. A replacement is $42,000, the old van trades at $4,500, and you expect eight years out of the new one, which should need about $700 of servicing a year and be down about a day.

LineAmount
Repairs$6,400
Downtime (14 × $900)$12,600
Cost of keeping$19,000 / yr
Net capital ($42,000 − $4,500)$37,500
Annualised over 8 years$4,687.50
Servicing on the new van$700
Downtime on the new van (1 × $900)$900
Cost of replacing$6,287.50 / yr
Annual saving from replacing$12,712.50
Repair + downtime spend it stops$17,400 / yr
Payback ($37,500 ÷ $17,400)about 2.16 years

Payback divides the capital by the spend it stops — $19,000 of repairs and downtime less the $1,600 the new van still costs to run. It deliberately does not use the $12,712.50 annual saving above: that figure already has the capital spread through it, so dividing the capital by it would charge the purchase for itself twice.

Note what happens if you drop the downtime line: keeping costs $6,400, replacing costs $6,287.50, and the decision looks like a coin toss you would probably resolve by keeping the van. The downtime is the whole argument.

And the reverse case is just as real. A 2021 van with $900 of repairs, two days down, and a $21,000 trade-in costs about $2,700 a year to keep against $4,125 to replace. That one you keep, and a planner that could never say so would just be a sales tool.

Which one first, when you cannot do all of them

With one budget and several candidates, the instinct is to start with the oldest, or with the biggest repair bill. Both can be wrong. An old machine with a huge repair bill can still be the wrong first move if its replacement is expensive and its trade-in is worthless.

Rank by annual saving per dollar of capital instead:

saving per dollar = annual saving / net capital

In the example above the van returns $0.34 a year per dollar of capital. A mini excavator saving $7,600 a year on $49,000 of capital returns $0.16 — a real saving, and still the second thing you do, not the first. Work down that list until the budget runs out, then look at what deferring the rest costs you per year and compare it against what the extra capital would cost you to borrow. Sometimes borrowing is obviously worth it; the point is to see the number rather than guess at it.

Strictly, filling a fixed budget is a knapsack problem and ranking by ratio is a heuristic rather than a guaranteed-best answer. With a handful of assets it is almost always the best or near-best split, and it has the advantage that you can see why each asset sits where it does.

What this arithmetic deliberately ignores

  • Financing interest and the time value of money. Capital is spread straight-line. If you would borrow, add your own cost of borrowing before you decide.
  • Tax and depreciation. Write-offs can move a marginal case either way, and they depend on your position, not on this page.
  • Everything that is not money. A vehicle your crew trusts, or one that is still under warranty, or a machine you cannot get delivered until next spring — those are real and they are yours to weigh.

The arithmetic is deliberately simple enough to check on paper, because a number you cannot check is a number you should not commit capital on.

Run your own fleet through the planner →

vs-comparing-the-repair-bill-to-a-new-pr.text:
← Fleet repair-or-replace planner

This planner vs. comparing the repair bill to a new price

The default way owners make this call is holding this year's repair invoice up against the price of a new one. That comparison is not wrong, exactly -- it is incomplete. It leaves out downtime, the resale value a trade-in would return, and how several assets stack against one capital budget. This free planner adds all three, per asset, in the same worksheet.

What each one leaves in, and out

Repair bill vs. new price is the comparison most owners already run in their head, and it costs nothing: this year's invoices against a dealer quote. What it cannot see is the vehicle sitting in the shop while the crew works around it -- days that are billable revenue lost, not a repair line item -- and it treats the new price as the whole cost, ignoring what a trade-in would return and that the purchase buys several years of service, not one.

This planner runs the same comparison with those three pieces added: downtime valued at what you say a day off the road costs you, the new asset's price netted against its resale value and spread over its expected service life, and -- once you have more than one asset -- a ranking of which ones actually pay to replace against a fixed capital budget. See why downtime decides this for the arithmetic worked through on a real fleet.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Is the repair bill bigger than a new price, roughly?The comparison every owner already runs -- free, but leaves out downtime and resale.
What does keeping this asset really cost once downtime is counted?This planner's per-asset arithmetic.
Which of several assets actually pay to replace against one budget?This planner -- a repair-bill comparison cannot rank a fleet at all.
Is my data uploaded anywhere?No. Everything stays in this browser tab; nothing is sent to a server.

A repair-bill comparison is a reasonable first filter for one vehicle you are not seriously considering replacing -- if the invoice is small, there is often no need to run the arithmetic at all. It stops being enough the moment downtime is significant, a trade-in is on the table, or there is more than one asset competing for the same capital.

This planner needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and nothing you type is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

What's wrong with just comparing the repair bill to a new price?

Nothing is wrong with looking at both numbers — the problem is what that comparison leaves out. The repair invoice is the visible cost, but a vehicle in the shop is also billable days your crew could not work, and that downtime is frequently the larger number. It leaves out resale value, since a trade-in offsets the new price. And it leaves out spreading the purchase over the years of service it buys, so a $42,000 truck and a $68,000 excavator are not directly comparable on price alone. This planner adds all three to the same comparison, per asset.

Why not just eyeball it — if the repairs are getting expensive, replace it?

Because 'getting expensive' has no threshold, and the two numbers that actually decide the answer — downtime cost and the replacement's equivalent annual cost — are not the ones a repair invoice shows. An owner going on the invoice alone can keep the wrong asset (heavy downtime, cheap repairs) and replace the wrong one (expensive repairs, but rarely down) in the same year. The arithmetic takes the same two minutes as eyeballing it once the figures are in front of you.

I only have one truck to decide about — do I still need a tool for this?

The single-asset arithmetic is short enough to run on paper once you know it — see the worked example on the explainer page. Where a tool earns its keep is a fleet of several vehicles and machines and one capital budget: ranking which ones actually pay to replace, and in what order, is not something a repair-bill-vs-new-price comparison can do at all, because it never puts the assets on the same footing.

Does this planner tell me the right answer?

No — it runs arithmetic on the figures you enter and shows its work. It does not appraise your equipment, know your financing terms, or decide anything for you. It replaces a comparison that leaves out downtime and resale, not your judgment about the quotes and trade-in values you confirm before committing capital.

vs-fleet-management-software.html.text:
← Fleet repair-or-replace planner

This planner vs. paid fleet management software

Paid fleet management/maintenance software tracks every vehicle continuously, for a recurring per-vehicle fee. This free tool does one narrower thing, whenever you need it: rank which assets actually pay to replace this year against a fixed capital budget, valuing the downtime days most owners leave out.

What each one is for

Paid fleet management/maintenance software — the category that includes work-order tracking, inspection checklists, service scheduling, and often telematics or fuel-card integration — is built for continuous, day-to-day record-keeping across a fleet, usually priced per vehicle per month. It is the right tool once you are managing enough vehicles that ongoing tracking justifies the subscription.

This planner is a free, single-purpose worksheet for one recurring decision: given the repair spend and downtime you already know for each vehicle or machine, which ones actually pay to replace this year, and in what order against your capital budget. It holds no vehicle database, schedules no maintenance, and forgets your figures on refresh unless you export them.

See why downtime decides this for the arithmetic this planner runs.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Do I need ongoing service records, inspections, or driver logs for my fleet?Fleet management software — this planner keeps none of that.
Which of my vehicles actually pay to replace this year, given a fixed capital budget?This planner — free, in your browser, no account.
What does keeping an asset really cost once downtime is counted?This planner's per-asset arithmetic.
Should I track fuel, mileage, or telematics across my fleet day to day?A different, larger decision this planner does not address.
Is my data uploaded anywhere?No. Everything stays in this browser tab; nothing is sent to a server.

A fleet already paying for management software can still use this planner for the annual capital-budget decision: pull each vehicle's repair spend from the software's own records, estimate downtime days from memory or the software's out-of-service log, and run the comparison here. The two are complementary rather than competing.

This planner needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and nothing you type is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Should I use this planner or paid fleet management software?

They answer different questions. Fleet management/maintenance software tracks every vehicle continuously — work orders, service history, inspections, sometimes telematics — for a recurring per-vehicle fee, and is worth it once you are managing enough vehicles that continuous tracking pays for itself. This planner does one narrower thing, for free, whenever you need it: given the repair spend and downtime you already know for each asset, which ones actually pay to replace this year, and in what order against your capital budget. A small fleet can use this planner without ever paying for ongoing tracking software; a larger one often uses both — the software for day-to-day records, this planner for the annual capital-budget decision.

Does this replace fleet management software?

No, and it is not built to. This planner has no vehicle database, no maintenance scheduling, no inspection checklists, no telematics, and no multi-user access — it holds only what you type in for one planning session, in your own browser, and forgets it on refresh unless you export it. If you need ongoing service records, driver logs, or fuel and mileage tracking across a fleet, that is what fleet management software is for.

Why not just use the repair-vs-replace report my fleet software already generates?

Check what it actually reports first. Many fleet-software repair-cost views total maintenance spend per vehicle, which is only half of this decision — the other half, downtime cost, usually is not tracked as a dollar figure at all because it depends on what your crew would have billed that day, something fleet software does not know. This planner asks for that number directly and puts it in the same comparison as the repair spend and the replacement's equivalent annual cost, then ranks the whole fleet against one capital budget.

Is this planner free because it is a stripped-down version of a paid product?

No — there is no paid tier, no vehicle limit, and no upsell. It is a static, client-side worksheet with one job: cost repair-or-replace including downtime, then rank a fleet against a budget. It does not compete with fleet management software's actual job, which is continuous, multi-user record-keeping this tool was never built to do.

vs-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Fleet repair-or-replace planner

This planner vs. a spreadsheet

This decision fits a spreadsheet's shape: one row per asset, a keep-cost formula, a replace-cost formula, a rank column against a budget. This page names no specific product — it compares against the generic method of building that sheet yourself, not a competing calculator.

What each one is for

A spreadsheet can run every formula this planner runs. Nothing here is beyond ordinary spreadsheet arithmetic. What a spreadsheet does not do on its own is keep the payback formula non-circular once it is written, or re-check that the ranking still fills the budget correctly after a row is added, removed, or re-priced.

This planner runs the same equivalent-annual-cost comparison and the same saving-per-dollar ranking for every asset you enter, states the assumptions behind them next to the numbers, and exports the full table as CSV — no formula to write, copy down, or re-derive after the fleet changes.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Can I build this in a spreadsheet?Yes — the formulas are ordinary, if every row's stays right.
Does payback divide by the annual saving or by the cash freed up?The cash freed up. Dividing by the annual saving after capital is already subtracted counts the purchase twice and understates how fast it pays back.
Does filling the budget by total saving find the best subset?No — rank by saving per dollar of capital, or a few large assets crowd out several smaller, better-returning ones.
Can I hand someone the full table without re-deriving it?This planner's CSV export, not a shared spreadsheet link.
Is my data uploaded anywhere?No. Everything stays in this browser tab; nothing is sent to a server.

Common questions

Can a spreadsheet do this repair-or-replace comparison?

Yes, in principle: one row per vehicle or machine, a formula for the annual cost of keeping it (repair spend plus downtime days times what a day off the road costs you), a formula for the annual cost of replacing it (net capital spread over its expected service life, plus what the new asset still costs to run), and a rank column to fill a capital budget. Every part of that is ordinary spreadsheet arithmetic. Where it goes wrong is not the formula being hard to write once — it is keeping all of it right across every row, every year, as assets are added, sold, or re-priced.

Where does a hand-built version usually go wrong?

Two places, both easy to get right once and wrong later. First, payback: the honest formula divides the capital outlay by the cash you stop spending each year on repairs and downtime — not by the annual saving after the new asset's own capital cost is already subtracted, which charges the purchase for itself twice and makes a genuinely fast payback look years slower than it is. Second, the ranking: filling a fixed budget by total saving instead of saving per dollar of capital spends the same money on fewer, larger assets and leaves smaller, better-returning ones unfunded. Neither mistake throws an error. The sheet just quietly recommends the wrong thing.

What does this planner do that a spreadsheet does not do for you?

It runs the same equivalent-annual-cost formula, the same non-circular payback formula, and the same saving-per-dollar ranking against your capital budget every time, for every row, with no formula to copy down and no cell reference that can silently point at the wrong row after an asset is added or removed. It also states its own assumptions — straight-line capital with no financing interest, resale valued in the year of purchase, a greedy rather than guaranteed-optimal budget fill — next to the numbers, rather than leaving them implicit in a formula only its author remembers.

If I already track my fleet in a spreadsheet, do I need to switch?

No. Keep the spreadsheet for whatever else it already does — a maintenance log, a mileage tracker, a list of assets. Pull each asset's repair spend and downtime days from it into this planner once a year for the capital-budget decision itself, where getting the payback formula and the ranking right matters most, then go back to the spreadsheet for everything else.

Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?

No. This planner runs entirely in your browser; nothing you type is uploaded.

Open the repair-or-replace planner, or read why downtime decides this.
